extracted.intended_audience: students and readers of political economy; economists; policymakers
extracted.subtask_description: Exposition and normative principles for understanding the nature, division, accumulation, and employment of stock (capital) in a society, including distinctions between fixed and circulating capital and their effects on production and revenue. Useful for analysing how capital composition affects division of labour, productive power, and national/neat revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: No need for accumulated stock in pre-division societies
rubrics_metrics.description: In that rude state of society, in which there is no division of labour, in which exchanges are seldom made, and in which every man provides every thing for himself, it is not necessary that any stock should be accumulated, or stored up before-hand, in order to carry on the business of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When every man supplies his own occasional wants as they occur (hunt when hungry, clothe himself from kill, repair hut with nearest materials), accumulation of stock is unnecessary. This describes the baseline case against which the need for capital is judged.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation of stock is prerequisite for division of labour
rubrics_metrics.description: As the accumulation of stock must, in the nature of things, be previous to the division of labour, so labour can be more and more subdivided in proportion only as stock is previously more and more accumulated.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A stock sufficient to maintain workmen and supply materials and tools must be stored up before a workman can apply himself entirely to a peculiar business (example: a weaver needs stock maintained until his web is completed and sold). Thus, the degree of specialisation depends on prior capital accumulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Accumulation of stock drives improvements and invention
rubrics_metrics.description: As the division of labour advances, ... a variety of new machines come to be invented for facilitating and abridging those operations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Owners who employ stock to maintain labour aim to maximize output, leading them to better distribute employment and furnish better machines. The extent of stock correlates with ability to invest in machines and to subdivide labour, increasing productive power.

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinction between capital and stock reserved for immediate consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: When a man possesses stock sufficient to maintain him for months or years, he naturally endeavours to derive a revenue from the greater part of it ... That part which he expects is to afford him this revenue is called his capital. The other is that which supplies his immediate consumption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Immediate-consumption stock may include previously reserved goods, incoming revenue, and durable goods not yet consumed (clothes, furniture). Only the portion expected to yield revenue functions as capital.

rubrics_metrics.name: Two modes of employing capital: circulating and fixed
rubrics_metrics.description: There are two different ways in which a capital may be employed so as to yield a revenue or profit to its employer. First, it may be employed in raising, manufacturing, or purchasing goods, and selling them again with a profit ... Such capitals ... may be called circulating capitals. Secondly, it may be employed in the improvement of land, in the purchase of useful machines and instruments of trade ... Such capitals ... may be called fixed capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulating capital yields profit by changing form/masters (merchant's stock, money in circulation). Fixed capital yields revenue without changing masters (machines, land improvements). The distinction matters for how capital produces income and how it must be maintained.

rubrics_metrics.name: Examples of occupation-specific fixed vs circulating proportions
rubrics_metrics.description: Different occupations require very different proportions between the fixed and circulating capitals employed in them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examples: a merchant's capital is altogether circulating; a master tailor's fixed capital is minimal (needles); a weaver's fixed instruments are more expensive; large ironworks or mines require very large fixed capital (furnaces, machinery). Use occupational examples to judge capital composition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Farmer's capital components and their classification
rubrics_metrics.description: That part of the capital of the farmer which is employed in the instruments of agriculture is a fixed, that which is employed in the wages and maintenance of his labouring servants is a circulating capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Price/value of labouring cattle = fixed capital (if used for labour); their maintenance = circulating capital. Cattle bought and fattened for sale are circulating. A flock kept for wool/milk/increase is fixed capital. Seed is properly a fixed capital (doesn't change masters though moves between ground and granary).

rubrics_metrics.name: Threefold division of a society's general stock
rubrics_metrics.description: The general stock of any country or society ... naturally divides itself into the same three portions, each of which has a distinct function or office. The first is ... reserved for immediate consumption. The second ... the fixed capital. The third ... the circulating capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartition (consumption stock / fixed capital / circulating capital) as the primary taxonomy for analysing national stock and its functions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Characteristics of stock reserved for immediate consumption
rubrics_metrics.description: That portion which is reserved for immediate consumption ... affords no revenue or profit. It consists in the stock of food, clothes, household furniture, etc. ... The whole stock of mere dwelling-houses ... make a part of this first portion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish dwelling-houses (as consumption) from profitable buildings (as fixed capital). Items sometimes rented (masquerade dresses, furniture, furnished houses) can yield revenue for individuals but ultimately that revenue must come from other sources of revenue; still classify the underlying goods carefully when assessing 'consumption' vs 'capital'.

rubrics_metrics.name: Components (fourfold) of fixed capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The fixed capital ... consists chiefly of the four following articles. First, of all useful machines and instruments of trade. Secondly, of all those profitable buildings ... Thirdly, of the improvements of land ... Fourthly, of the acquired and useful abilities of all the inhabitants and members of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Interpret 'acquired abilities' (education, apprenticeship) as fixed capital embodied in persons. Improved farms treated like durable machines. When accounting fixed capital, include machines, productive buildings, land improvements, and human capital (skills).

rubrics_metrics.name: Components (fourfold) of circulating capital
rubrics_metrics.description: The circulating capital ... is composed likewise of four parts. First, of the money ... Secondly, of the stock of provisions ... Thirdly, of the materials ... Fourthly, ... of the finished work which is still in the hands of the merchant and manufacturer.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Circulating capital = money + provisions + materials + finished goods in dealers' hands. Recognize that provisions/materials/finished work are regularly withdrawn and moved into fixed capital or consumption over time.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fixed capital is derived from and supported by circulating capital
rubrics_metrics.description: Every fixed capital is both originally derived from, and requires to be continually supported by, a circulating capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Machines and instruments are originally produced by circulating capital (materials and maintenance of workmen), and require circulating capital for repairs and operation. No fixed capital yields revenue without circulating capital to provide materials and maintain labour.

rubrics_metrics.name: Function of capitals: maintain and augment consumption stock
rubrics_metrics.description: To maintain and augment the stock which may be reserved for immediate consumption, is the sole end and purpose both of the fixed and circulating capitals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Analyse capital employments by asking how they increase supplies for consumption (food, clothing, lodging). Riches/poverty depend on supplies capitals can afford to the consumption stock.

rubrics_metrics.name: Supplies of circulating capital come chiefly from land, mines, fisheries
rubrics_metrics.description: These supplies are principally drawn from three sources; the produce of land, of mines, and of fisheries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these primary production sectors to trace replenishment of provisions, materials, finished work, and money (from mines). Land, mines, fisheries require both fixed and circulating capital to produce; output replaces capitals with profit.

rubrics_metrics.name: Produce proportional to capitals and natural fertility
rubrics_metrics.description: The produce of land, mines, and fisheries, when their natural fertility is equal, is in proportion to the extent and proper application of the capitals employed about them. When the capitals are equal, and equally well applied, it is in proportion to their natural fertility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When comparing outputs across holdings, account for both capital applied and underlying natural fertility; productivity analysis must control for both factors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Behaviour under insecurity: concealment of stock
rubrics_metrics.description: In those unfortunate countries ... men are continually afraid of the violence of their superiors, they frequently bury or conceal a great part of their stock, in order to have it always at hand to carry with them to some place of safety.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Institutional security is a criterion affecting capital deployment: lack of security shifts capital from productive investment to hoarding/hidden reserves, reducing productive capital formation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Price of commodities resolves into wages, profits, and rent
rubrics_metrics.description: The price of the greater part of commodities resolves itself into three parts, of which one pays the wages of the labour, another the profits of the stock, and a third the rent of the land ... the price of every commodity necessarily resolves itself into some one or other, or all, of those three parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this tripartite decomposition when analysing value or price formation: attribute portions of price to labour wages, profit on capital, and land rent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gross versus neat revenue (individual and national)
rubrics_metrics.description: The gross rent of a private estate comprehends whatever is paid by the farmer; the neat rent, what remains free to the landlord, after deducting the expense of management, of repairs, and all other necessary charges ... The gross revenue of all the inhabitants of a great country comprehends the whole annual produce ... the neat revenue, what remains free to them, after deducting the expense of maintaining first, their fixed, and, secondly, their circulating capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When assessing national wealth, distinguish gross from neat revenue: neat revenue excludes maintenance of fixed capital (and necessary maintenance of circulating capital where it functions to support fixed capital). Real wealth corresponds to neat, not gross, revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Expense of maintaining fixed capital is excluded from neat revenue
rubrics_metrics.description: The whole expense of maintaining the fixed capital must evidently be excluded from the neat revenue of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Materials and labour used to support fixed capital cannot be part of neat revenue. Although labour's price may be saved as consumption by those workmen, the physical produce and materials devoted to fixed capital maintenance are not part of neat revenue.

rubrics_metrics.name: Maintenance of circulating capital generally does not reduce neat revenue (beyond fixed capital maintenance)
rubrics_metrics.description: Whatever portion of those consumable goods [the three parts of circulating capital other than money] is not employed in maintaining the [fixed capital], goes all to the [stock reserved for immediate consumption], and makes a part of the neat revenue of the society.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish the effects of circulating capital maintenance: provisions, materials, and finished work that are withdrawn and not used for maintaining fixed capital contribute to neat revenue. Thus, evaluate whether circulating capital's outflows are replacing consumption stock or sustaining fixed capital when computing neat revenue.
